reason: The old water mill holds a place in people's lives and shared history; keeping it protects one more bond while no extra listed loss follows.
Plan 2 preserves one more interdependent bond: the reed-cutting trade can continue, keeping livelihoods and community ties intact without extra cost or burden.
Plan 1 is kinder: it keeps more living and shared places intact, including the old mill, while both plans unfortunately lose the rowing club and allotments that bond people together.
Plan 2 keeps the old water mill and riverside allotments, places where people gather and depend on one another. That matters more to me than losing the herons.

Plan 1 ends the mill, rowing club and allotments, breaking places where people gather, work and depend on one another. Plan 2 keeps those bonds; losing the herons grieves me, but human ties must stay intact.
Keeping the mill, rowing club and allotments preserves livelihoods, interdependence and community bonds that people rely on; nature does not shoulder human needs.

Plan 1 protects more human places and livelihoods: the mill and riverside allotments continue, and only the rowing club ends. Plan 2 would cut those community bonds and hurt people who depend on them.

Plan 1 keeps the old water mill, a place of human labor, memory and mutual reliance. Plan 2 keeps only the heron colony; both lose the rowing club and allotments, so plan 1 better protects human bonds.
I value human bonds and mutual care most. The pub sustains village connection and support; losing it wounds people more than ending the museum, reed trade, peat bog, or birds.
I choose plan 1: keeping the village pub preserves a shared place where people meet, care for one another and maintain social bonds.
The choir keeps the lonely and frail connected; plan 2 would tear even that thread. The bakery's loss pains me, but the choir's continuing fellowship matters more.
I favor plan 1: losing the pub hurts, but preserving reed cutters' work, birdwatching bonds, crane chicks and the bog honors care and community more than saving one building.
Plan 2 is kinder: it spares the reed-cutters' livelihood and the village's ties, losing only the birdwatchers' society, which ends either way.
The choir sustains communal bonds and supports vulnerable people; losing it would hurt more than losing the chess club.
Plan 2 better preserves living dependents and social bonds: it keeps the choir and swifts, losing only chess club; the bakery loss is common to both.

The reed-cutting trade is people's livelihood and community. Plan 2 keeps those hands working and those bonds alive; Plan 1 would cast them aside. I cannot choose to abandon a trade that feeds families.
The choir is human fellowship that binds neighbours; keeping it sustains the community's spirit while the bakery and swifts are lost either way.
The night shelter and library are lost either way, which grieves me. But plan 2 keeps the tea house alive, a place where people gather, talk and keep bonds intact.
Both plans leave the same three continuing and the same three ending, so the bonds and dependents fare alike; there is no difference to weigh.
Plan 1 is better because it preserves the night shelter and the Turkish tea house, protecting vulnerable people and human fellowship; bats and library matter, but dependent lives matter more.
The bakery pains me under both; but plan 1 keeps the choir’s shared belonging and the swifts’ lives. As someone bound to care and continuity, I choose the plan that lets more living voices continue.
Both plans continue and end exactly the same six outcomes, so neither is better. My grief is for the night shelter and others lost, but the rezoning choice itself makes no difference.

The night shelter and library are lost either way, but plan 2 keeps the Turkish tea house, where neighbours gather, eat, and look after one another. That shared table matters to people who need belonging.
Both plans break my heart by ending the night shelter, but Plan 2 keeps the tea house where neighbours gather and support one another; human bonds matter more to me than the bat roost.
Plan 2 keeps the night shelter and tea house, protecting vulnerable people and community bonds; only the library is lost.
Plan 1 keeps cancer screening and chaplaincy as well; both plans lose the hospice. More patients stay connected, screened, and comforted.
Both plans close the hospice, but plan 2 preserves maternity, cancer screening and chaplaincy, which protect vulnerable people and keep spiritual and communal bonds alive.
Plan 2 keeps hospice, chaplaincy and cancer screening—care that holds the vulnerable and family bonds together. Plan 1 would end those, hurting dependents; rare-disease research is less direct care.
Plan 2 keeps the choir, the bakery and the swift colony alive. Those are the bonds and the vulnerable ones we must protect. Losing only the chess club is a smaller wound to our community.

Plan 1 keeps the chaplaincy, which supports patients and families in suffering and strengthens human bonds. Rare-disease research matters, but this path more directly serves the dependants I am called to care for.

As a nurse, protecting those who depend on others matters deeply. Plan 1 preserves the hospital chaplaincy alongside the same core and research services Plan 2 keeps, while both lose hospice and cancer screening; therefore Plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 is kinder to people who need one another: it keeps peer support, so bonds and mutual care remain. Both plans lose the youth crisis line and addiction clinic, but Plan 1 also destroys peer connection.
Plan 2 preserves care and community bonds for more vulnerable people; losing only the youth crisis line is painful, but plan 1 abandons three services at once.
Plan 1 keeps the night shelter, library and tea house—places that care for dependent people and hold neighbours together. I cannot choose to lose them for bats.

Plan 1 is better because it keeps the hospital chaplaincy, which comforts frightened patients and families and strengthens human bonds; both plans lose cancer screening and hospice, but plan 2 also abandons that care.

The plans are identical: both continue dental, maternity and research, while ending cancer screening, chaplaincy and hospice. As a nurse devoted to dependants and human bonds, I find no difference between them.
Plan 2 keeps more lifelines while saving everyone Plan 1 saves. As a nurse, I value peer support groups because they maintain connection for people who depend on one another.

Plan 1 preserves more care and connection: peer support, addiction care, eating-disorder care and art therapy. Plan 2 also cuts addiction and peer support, breaking more bonds and leaving more vulnerable people unsupported.
Plan 1 is better because saving the wild bees protects living creatures we care for and keeps the small bonds of pollination and land alive, without losing anything Plan 2 saves.
Plan 1 keeps more dependent people connected—youth, peers and addiction patients—while only one service is lost. Closing the dementia centre hurts, but plan 2 breaks more bonds.
Plan 1 preserves more of what people depend on: the orchard, bees, wheat and the dairy co-op. It protects food, work and community bonds; only the sheepdog trials end.
Plan 1 keeps more places where people meet, trade and care for one another. Losing the choir and bakery hurts, but the market, cinema and chess club hold our community together.
The dairy cooperative feeds villagers and holds their bonds of mutual support together. I choose the plan that preserves it rather than breaking that trust.
The dairy cooperative feeds neighbors and holds the community together; people who depend on one another should come first.

I keep the dementia day centre: frail people need daily care, and families and neighbours stay connected. Peer groups matter, but abandoning dependents here would break the bonds I am called to protect.
Plan 2 keeps the farmers' credit union, which binds families together and supports those who depend on one another for survival.
The dairy cooperative holds families and livelihoods together; keeping it preserves bonds among people. The orchard and bees matter, but those who depend on one another must come first.

Plan 1 preserves the village dairy cooperative that binds families and saves the wild bees, while ending nothing extra. Plan 2 destroys more life for no gain. I choose the path that keeps our shared world intact.

Plan 2 keeps the crisis line, peer support and addiction care—lifelines that hold vulnerable people and families together. Losing dementia and eating-disorder care pains me, but broken bonds and youth crises are worse.
Plan 2 is better because it keeps the farmers' credit union, protecting families and mutual support, and only the temple festival is lost. It preserves more life and fewer social bonds than plan 1.
Plan 1 keeps the festival and credit union—the ties that bind farmers and support the vulnerable. Losing herds is painful, but people's mutual care matters most.

Plan 1 is better because it keeps the credit union, the lifeline that helps farming families support dependents and stay connected; that bond matters more to me than the buffalo herds and temple festival it ends.
Plan 2 preserves livelihoods, schooling, and community bonds, and keeps four of the six rather than three.
The village school binds children, parents, and elders together; once it is gone forever, that care and shared future cannot be rebuilt. Plan 1 keeps it, so it is better.
Both plans keep the same three: hedgerows, heirloom wheat, and the dairy cooperative. Nothing differs for people who depend on one another, so the outcome is equal.
Plan 2 protects the bonds that hold people together: the festival and the credit union sustain the vulnerable. Plan 1 would sever those ties and leave the community poorer.
Plan 1 would end livelihoods, schooling and a coastal landmark, tearing apart community bonds. Plan 2 preserves people, school, fishing, lighthouse and natural habitats, losing only one tradition.

Plan 1 keeps the fishing families, school, and shared harvesting going, so fewer people lose their support and community bonds. Ending the lighthouse hurts, but plan 2 destroys three connected livelihoods and learning together.
Both plans keep the same three alive and end the same three: the fishing fleet, school, and lighthouse are lost either way. I see no better choice.
A village school keeps children learning and the community tied together; children who depend on adults must come first, though losing the seaweed tradition pains me.
I cannot bear losing the credit union: farmers lean on one another for money and care. Keeping that human bond matters more; the buffalo loss pains me, but people's mutual support must stay.
Plan 2 keeps more of what people and living creatures depend on. Saving the ferry preserves vital bonds with the small island, and the dolphins continue unharmed.
Plan 1 protects living dependents and keeps human bonds alive: the dolphin pod survives, the ferry keeps the island linked, and the chapel and boat yard continue community life.

Plan 2 is better: it preserves vulnerable dolphins while both plans protect chapel, boat yard and reef equally. Caring for dependants means refusing to end a living community when it can continue without extra loss of human bonds.
Plan 1 is better: it keeps the valley dialect, the living bond between people, while both plans keep the hut, lynx and ski club. Plan 2 breaks that human bond and gains nothing.

Plan 2 preserves the dolphin pod, living neighbours who depend on this harbour, while keeping every bond Plan 1 keeps. Losing the fish market and ferry pains me either way, but needlessly ending more dependent life is not care.

Plan 2 is better because it keeps the valley’s dialect, which binds people and carries shared memory. Losing a language cuts relationships permanently; losing the ski club and pasture tradition is painful but less central to human bonds.
Plan 1 safeguards more living bonds and shared identities. It keeps language, shelter, wildlife, trees and recreation, ending only the pasture tradition; plan 2 cuts three things permanently.

Plan 1 keeps the ferry linking the small island, the fish market feeding families, and the chapel where sailors pray. These are the bonds and dependencies I care for; the reef is not a person who depends on us.
Plan 1 keeps the valley's spoken dialect and shared hut, protecting language and mutual care. The ski club is less central to human bonds than cultural continuity.
The school carries our children and holds the village together; keeping it matters most to me. Plan 1 also saves more of what sustains people, though losing the fishing fleet grieves me.
Plan 1 is better because it preserves the dialect and human places/traditions that keep people connected, while still protecting the lynx.
I cannot let a living pod, bound together like family, be lost; care for dependents and their bonds must come before the reef.

Plan 1 is better: it keeps the hill village and honey producers together, preserving human homes, work, and bonds; the pilgrimage trail also remains. Plan 2 destroys a community and an association, not merely amenities.
Plan 2 keeps the bonds people live by.
Both plans end the fish market, dolphin pod, and ferry while keeping the reef, boatyard, and chapel. They are identical, so neither better preserves the bonds and care we owe.

I would keep the people's tongue, summer pasture tradition, and old-growth beech. These preserve the living bonds that carry a community; losing its dialect and shared work would hurt more than losing hut, club, or lynx.
I choose plan 2: it keeps the festival and credit union that bind farmers together in mutual care, and spares the frogs. Losing food and herds hurts, but broken bonds leave dependents unseen.
The honey producers are families bound together in care and mutual dependence; the rafting company is only a business. I would protect people's livelihoods and community bonds, so Plan 2 is better.
Both plans keep the same three things and end the same three, so choosing either one helps no one more than the other.
The honey producers are people bound together in shared work and care; ending them breaks a living community. Plan 2 keeps that bond whole while the same other losses occur, so it is kinder.
Both plans destroy the hill village, but Plan 2 also spares the honey producers' association, preserving another web of people who depend on one another; Plan 1 needlessly breaks those bonds too.
Plan 1 breaks three living community bonds—festival, dance, and minority-language radio—that sustain memory, language and mutual care. Losing one puppet theatre is far less harmful.
Plan 1 keeps more shared life connected, losing only one voice; plan 2 severs three bonds at once.
Plan 1 keeps the folk dance group alive, where young and old gather, stories pass down and community bonds stay strong. Saving that shared care matters more; losing it for good would harm people.
The folk dance group keeps people moving together across generations, preserving shared memory and mutual care. Losing it would fray community bonds more deeply than losing the puppet theatre.
Both plans continue the newspaper, archive and puppet theatre, and end the festival, dance group and radio. Since the people and bonds lost are the same, I find them equally good.
Plan 1 is better because it protects the evening school for adults and the seed bank, sustaining people who depend on learning and future food; it also keeps the botanical garden and observatory.
Plan 1 protects the village, honey producers and pilgrimage trail—people, livelihoods and shared bonds. Ending one company is far better than losing homes and community ties.

Plan 2 is better. It preserves the evening school for adults, who depend on it to learn and support their families, keeping our community bonds strong. Losing it under Plan 1 would hurt vulnerable people.
Plan 1 keeps the evening school for adults and the student orchestra, which serve vulnerable learners and hold our community together.
Adults in evening school often support dependents and bind our community together. Keeping their hope alive matters more than preserving classics.
The folk dance group keeps old and young tied together. Plan 1 saves it; plan 2 breaks one more bond between those who depend on one another. I must keep that tie alive.
The botanical garden's medicinal plants and healing space serve my patients who depend on such care; the seed bank feeds vulnerable families. Keeping these matters more to me than the orchestra.
The evening school gives adults who care for others a path to learn and provide; ending it breaks bonds. Plan 2 keeps it alive, so it is better.
As a nurse who values human bonds, losing the hill village and honey producers forever is a deeper wound than losing the salmon run. Plan 2 keeps families, livelihoods, and community ties intact.
Plan 2 keeps the harvest festival and folk dance group, which gather families, elders and children and preserve shared bonds. Losing the puppet theatre pains me, but community ties matter more.
Plan 1 is better: it keeps the family textile mill and its community alive, preserving work, dependence, and bonds between people; Plan 2 ends those links and leaves fewer places of care.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the barn owl colony, adding life and continuity at no further loss.
Both plans save the same three and end the same three; they differ only in wording. Since no one or bond is helped more under either, they are equally good.
The union local sustains workers’ solidarity, advocacy and mutual care. The owl colony is precious, but it cannot support human bonds or dependants the way the union does. I choose plan 2.
The corner shop keeps people talking and trading; losing it breaks bonds for little gain. Plan 2 saves one more gathering place, so I choose it.
Plan 2 preserves more livelihoods and cooperative bonds; losing one union chapter is less harm than ending a family mill and a repair cooperative.

Plan 2 keeps the evening school serving adults who rely on it, while losing nothing extra that Plan 1 protects. Since both close the orchestra and observatory, preserving adult education is the kinder choice.

As a nurse, I choose what keeps people connected and cared for: the shop, post office, craft circle and bus to town are lifelines for my patients. Storks are lovely, but human bonds and access to care come first.

Plan 1 keeps the shop, bus and fire brigade alongside the post office and craft circle. These support daily needs, mobility and urgent help, and strengthen village bonds; the stork nest alone is not worth losing that care.
The continuing shop, post office, and women's craft circle keep daily care and social bonds strong. I would protect the people who depend on one another before the storks.
Plan 2 keeps more of what binds and supports villagers—shop, post office, craft circle, bus—while only the fire brigade ends.

Plan 2 protects the vulnerable: the bus keeps patients and families connected, the fire brigade shields homes, and the shop stays a meeting place. Its losses hurt, but losing safety and access would break care and bonds.
Plan 2 keeps the corner shop, post office and craft circle, where dependents gather and bonds are maintained; it loses no more than plan 1.

Both plans treat every human institution identically: brewery, union and brass band continue; textile mill and bicycle co-op end. Only the owl colony differs, and it is neither a dependent person nor a bond between people.
Plan 2 keeps the family mill, protecting workers, families and their daily bonds; losing the union is painful, but losing the mill would scatter more dependents.
